item.title: Curated Catalog of Open-Source MLSecOps Tools for AI Security
item.description:
Curated Catalog of Open-Source MLSecOps Tools for AI Security

A new curated catalog has been released to help security engineers, machine learning practitioners, developers, and AI red teams discover resources for integrating security into the machine learning lifecycle.

🔍 Overview

MLSecOps (Machine Learning Security Operations) is the practice of integrating security throughout the machine learning lifecycle, spanning data collection, model development, deployment, monitoring, and incident response. This catalog compiles open-source tools, adversarial machine learning research, AI security frameworks, threat-modeling resources, and practical learning materials to support these efforts.

🧩 How it works

The catalog applies security testing, threat modeling, supply-chain protection, access controls, and continuous monitoring to machine learning models, MLOps pipelines, LLM applications, and AI agents. The resources are organized into specific functional categories:

Category Function
Model and artifact security tools Detect unsafe serialization, malicious payloads, integrity failures, and other risks in machine learning model files.
Adversarial machine learning testing tools Evaluate model robustness against evasion, poisoning, extraction, inversion, and other adversarial techniques.
Embodied AI and robotics ML security tools Test policies that emit actions rather than text, where a successful attack moves a robot out of its safe envelope rather than changing a prediction.

💡 Why it matters

Open-source MLSecOps tools allow practitioners to test, monitor, and protect machine learning models, data, pipelines, LLM applications, and AI agents. The catalog serves as a central discovery point for these resources, including active projects and proofs of concept.

⚙️ Key details

  • The collection includes a mix of active projects and proofs of concept.
  • Users are advised to evaluate maintenance status, licensing, threat coverage, and deployment suitability before production use.
  • The newsletter for the MLSecOps Hacker focuses on model supply-chain security (serialization, signing, provenance), prompt injection, and agent and MCP security.

#MLSecOps #AISecurity #MLOps #OpenSource #ThreatModeling

Source: RiccardoBiosas/awesome-MLSecOps

item.title: New independent guide provides catalog of twenty LLM security and red teaming tools
item.description:
New independent guide provides catalog of twenty LLM security and red teaming tools

An independent evaluation guide has been released featuring 20 synced entries from the community-maintained Awesome MLSecOps catalog. This resource provides a central list of tools designed to find weaknesses in Large Language Model (LLM) applications that conventional application scanners cannot detect.

🔍 Overview

LLM security tools help teams exercise various components of Gen AI applications under adversarial input. These tools are designed to test model behavior, system prompts, retrieval pipelines, tool calls, output handling, and policy controls. The catalog serves as a discovery aid rather than a security certification, helping users find resources directly from the community rather than through paid placement programs.

⚙️ Key details

The tools listed in the guide support several security and testing functions for generative AI:

  • Prompt-injection testing: Identifying vulnerabilities to malicious instructions.
  • Jailbreak evaluation: Checking model guardrails against abuse.
  • Sensitive-data leakage checks: Validating that models do not expose protected information.
  • Guardrail validation: Testing programmable barriers between application code and the LLM.
  • Repeatable red-team campaigns: Organizing offensive security tests against applications.

🚀 Availability

The following tools and frameworks are included in the guide, with descriptions maintained from the Awesome MLSecOps repository:

Tool Name Description
AI Goat A Large Language Model designed for getting hacked and vulnerable LLM CTF challenges.
NeMo Guardrails Programmable guardrails for developers to add between application code and the LLM.
Meta’s suite Safety and security tooling including Llama Guard, Code Shield, and CyberSecEval.
Python Risk Identification Tool A tool for identifying risks in generative AI applications.
Generative Application Firewall (GAF) An open-source firewall for protecting generative AI applications.
Repello AI tool An open-source offensive tool for testing against system prompt leakage.
Self-hostable DLP gateway Enterprise prompt gateway for ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini using Squid, Go ICAP, and mTLS.
Bias Tester A framework for testing bias in LLMs.
Prompt Injection CTF playground A playground for practicing prompt injection attacks.

💡 Why it matters

When choosing an LLM security tool, developers are advised to match the tool’s test library to their specific threat model and deployment architecture. These tools exercise application controls that traditional scanners may miss, providing specialized coverage for LLM-based systems.

#MLSecOps #Cybersecurity #LLM #RedTeaming #GenerativeAI

Source: LLM Security Tool Evaluation Guide | Awesome MLSecOps
